subject: rla
title: The Extended Response I: Evaluating Two Arguments, Planning, and Writing a Thesis
objectives: Students will explain what the GED Extended Response asks and how it is scored on three traits (creation of arguments and use of evidence; development of ideas and organizational structure; clarity and command of standard English), each worth 0 to 2 points.
Students will evaluate the evidence and reasoning in two opposing argument passages using five questions: source, specific, relevant, sufficient, and fair.
Students will decide which of two positions is better supported, based on evidence rather than personal opinion, and state that decision in a clear thesis.
Students will complete a planning organizer that gathers specific evidence from both passages.
Students will write a body paragraph that presents evidence and explains why it is strong or weak (Point, Evidence, Explain, Link).
teach:
Lesson overview

Week 9 prepares learners for the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts Extended Response: a 45-minute typed essay in which they read two passages that take opposite positions on an issue, decide which position is better supported, and explain why using evidence from both texts. This lesson focuses on the thinking and planning that come before writing: evaluating evidence and reasoning, choosing a side based on support (not personal opinion), writing a thesis, and organizing evidence from both passages. Week 10 focuses on organizing, revising, and editing a full draft. The skills from Week 5 (claims, evidence, reasoning, faulty reasoning) and Week 6 (comparing two texts) come together here, so remind learners that they already own most of the tools.

Objectives

  • Explain what the Extended Response asks and how it is scored (three traits, 0–2 points each).
  • Evaluate the evidence and reasoning in two opposing argument passages.
  • Decide which position is better supported and state that decision in a clear thesis.
  • Complete a planning organizer that pulls specific evidence from both passages.
  • Write a body paragraph that quotes or paraphrases evidence and explains why it is strong or weak.

Materials

  • Student Lesson, which contains the Port Delaney ballpark passages (Passage A and Passage B), the sample planning organizer, and the model response
  • This week’s Notes sheet, which includes the rubric summary
  • Blank planning organizers (draw a two-column table on paper: Claim, Key evidence, Quality, Flaws or appeals, Counterargument)
  • Highlighters in two colors (one for strong evidence, one for weak evidence or appeals)
  • A timer; computers or paper for typing or writing
  • Week 9 practice items (the Corbin Park turf passages, items 1–12)

60-minute timing plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5“Which would convince you?” Compare two pieces of evidence
Direct instruction20The task and the rubric; “better supported” vs. “I agree”; evaluating evidence; reading the ballpark passages; four worked examples
Guided practice15Bottle-deposit mini-pair: claims, strongest evidence, a flaw, a thesis; then complete the ballpark organizer together
Independent practice15Practice items 1–8 on the turf passages (items 9–12 for homework)
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding; exit ticket; assign the study plan

Warm-up (5 minutes): Which would convince you?

Read aloud: “A new gym opened on Main Street. You are deciding whether to buy a one-year membership.” Show two statements:

Statement 1: “My neighbor goes there, and she says it’s the best gym in town.”

Statement 2: “The gym surveyed 400 members after six months, and 82 percent said they planned to renew.”

Ask: Which is stronger evidence, and why? Is anything still missing?

Answers: Statement 2 is stronger because it is specific (a number), based on many people instead of one, and could be checked. It still has a weakness: the gym ran its own survey, so it has a reason to report good results. Statement 1 is one person’s opinion. Tell learners: “Today you will do exactly this, with two whole articles, and then write about it.”

Direct instruction (20 minutes)

1. The task (3 minutes)

Show the standard prompt wording and underline the key phrases: “In your response, analyze both positions presented in the articles to determine which one is best supported. Use relevant and specific evidence from both articles to support your response.” Talking points:

  • Each passage is usually a few hundred words long. Learners have 45 minutes to read, plan, type, and revise.
  • The question is not “Which side do you agree with?” It is “Which author proved it better?” A learner can personally disagree with the better-supported side and still write a top-scoring essay.
  • Either side can earn full credit if the essay uses strong evidence from the texts to show why that side is better supported. But usually one passage is clearly stronger, and choosing it makes the essay much easier to write.
  • Evidence must come from both passages: the strengths of one and the weaknesses of the other.

2. The rubric (4 minutes)

Show the table from the Student Lesson. Each trait is scored 0, 1, or 2.

  • Trait 1, Creation of arguments and use of evidence: Does the essay take a clear position on which argument is better supported, back it with specific, relevant evidence from both texts, and explain why the evidence is strong or weak?
  • Trait 2, Development of ideas and organizational structure: Do ideas build logically? Is there a clear introduction, body, and conclusion, with paragraphs that each have a job and transitions that connect them? Is the tone formal?
  • Trait 3, Clarity and command of standard English: Are sentences clear and varied? Are grammar, usage, capitalization, and punctuation mostly correct? Scorers expect a first draft written under time pressure, so a few minor errors are acceptable; errors that interfere with meaning are not.

Stress: an essay that only gives the writer’s opinion, or that does not use the passages, cannot score well on Trait 1, no matter how well it is written. An essay that is not about the passages, or copies large parts of them, can receive no credit at all.

3. How to judge “better supported” (5 minutes)

Review the Week 5 tests and add two more. For each piece of evidence, ask:

  1. Source: Who says so? Are they expert, independent, named? Do they gain from the outcome?
  2. Specific: Are there numbers, dates, measurements, or named studies, or just vague words like “many” or “everyone”?
  3. Relevant: Does it prove this claim, or something next to it?
  4. Sufficient: Is it enough? One story is not a pattern.
  5. Fair: Does the author deal with the other side honestly, or ignore or mock it?

Then list the faulty reasoning to watch for: hasty generalization (one case → a rule), bandwagon (“everyone agrees”), slippery slope (one step → disaster), appeal to emotion or pride in place of evidence, attacking the person, and unsupported claims (no source at all).

4. Read the ballpark passages (8 minutes, including the worked examples)

Have learners read Passage A and Passage B in the Student Lesson (Port Delaney ballpark). Learners highlight strong evidence in one color and weak evidence or appeals in another. Then model these four examples aloud.

Worked example 1: Evaluating one piece of evidence

Evidence: Bell, paragraph 2: “A study commissioned by the Pelicans found that the new ballpark would create 1,200 jobs and bring $30 million a year into the local economy.”

Step 1, Source: The Pelicans paid for the study. The Pelicans would get the new ballpark. The source gains from the result, so it may be biased.

Step 2, Specific: Yes, it has numbers, which makes it sound strong.

Step 3, Relevant: Yes, it speaks to the job claim.

Step 4, Check against the other passage: Osei (paragraph 3) points out that the team plays about 70 home games a year and that most ballpark jobs are part-time and seasonal, and that the study never says how many jobs are full-time.

Conclusion: Weak evidence. The numbers come from a source with a stake in the outcome, and the other passage shows what the numbers leave out. Teach the phrase: “Specific is not the same as reliable.”

Worked example 2: Spotting faulty reasoning

Evidence: Bell, paragraph 3: “My brother-in-law lives in Harlan City… He says downtown Harlan City is now packed with new restaurants and apartments. If it worked for Harlan City, it will work for us.”

Step 1: Who is the source? One relative, giving his impression. No data on jobs or income.

Step 2: Is it sufficient? No. It is one city, described secondhand. Even if downtown Harlan City grew, the passage gives no proof the stadium caused it.

Step 3: Name the flaw: hasty generalization (one example → a rule for every city).

Also in paragraph 5: “Everyone I talk to downtown is excited” is a bandwagon appeal; popularity does not prove a ballpark will help the economy. “Will pay for itself many times over” is an unsupported claim; Bell gives no figures.

Worked example 3: Writing a thesis

A thesis for the Extended Response does three things: names the better-supported side, says why in a short list of reasons, and refers to both authors.

  • Weak: “I think a ballpark is a waste of money.” (Personal opinion; does not mention the passages.)
  • Weak: “Both authors make good points.” (Takes no position.)
  • Better: “Osei’s argument is better supported.” (Takes a position but gives no reasons.)
  • Strong: “Osei’s argument is better supported because she relies on independent research and specific cost figures, while Bell relies on a team-funded study, one personal story, and appeals to pride.”

Point out that the strong thesis is also the outline: the “while Bell” part becomes one body paragraph and the “because she” part becomes another.

Worked example 4: Building an evidence paragraph (P-E-E-L)

Point: “Osei, on the other hand, supports her cost claim with clear numbers.”
Evidence: “She explains that the city would repay about $3.1 million a year for 25 years, about $77.5 million in all, while collecting only about $400,000 a year in rent.”
Explain: “These figures are specific and can be checked, and they show that the city would pay far more than it gets back.”
Link: “In contrast, Bell says the ballpark will ‘pay for itself many times over’ but never shows how.”

Quick check of the math with learners: $3.1 million × 25 = $77.5 million. The Explain step is where Trait 1 points are earned; never leave evidence without saying why it matters.

Guided practice (15 minutes)

Part 1 (7 minutes): Mini-pair. Read both short arguments aloud, then work the questions together.

Writer 1: Ashford should add a 10-cent deposit on bottles and cans. When neighboring Glen Ridge County added the same deposit in 2019, its public works department counted 58 percent fewer bottles and cans along county roadsides by 2022. Stores did need space for return machines, so Glen Ridge let small shops send returns to a central recycling center instead.

Writer 2: A bottle deposit is just another tax on working families. Everyone knows people will throw their bottles away anyway. Store owners I’ve met hate the idea. If we start charging deposits on bottles, soon there will be a fee on everything we buy.

  1. State each writer’s claim. Answer: Writer 1: Ashford should add a 10-cent deposit. Writer 2: Ashford should not.
  2. What is the strongest piece of evidence in either text? Answer: The Glen Ridge public works count: 58 percent fewer bottles and cans by 2022. It is specific, from a named official source, and relevant.
  3. Name two flaws in Writer 2. Answer: Any two: bandwagon/unsupported (“Everyone knows”), vague unnamed sources (“store owners I’ve met”), slippery slope (“soon there will be a fee on everything”), name-calling the deposit a “tax” without explaining (the money is returned when bottles are returned).
  4. How does Writer 1 handle the other side? Answer: Admits stores need space and explains Glen Ridge’s solution, which makes the argument more credible.
  5. Write a thesis. Sample answer: “Writer 1’s argument is better supported because it uses an official count from a nearby county and answers a likely objection, while Writer 2 relies on vague claims and a slippery slope.”

Part 2 (8 minutes): Ballpark organizer. Draw the blank organizer. Learners call out entries for each row; record them. Compare the result to the sample organizer in the Student Lesson. Expected entries match the sample: Bell’s evidence is the team-paid study, the Harlan City story, and the lease; Osei’s evidence is the independent studies, the $120 family example, the 70 home games, and the $77.5 million vs. $400,000 comparison. Then show the model response and have learners label its thesis, each P-E-E-L paragraph, and the counterargument paragraph.

Independent practice (15 minutes)

Learners complete practice items 1–8 on the Corbin Park artificial turf passages. Note for the teacher: in this pair, the pro side (the parks director) is better supported, while in the ballpark pair the con side was. Point this out at the end so learners do not assume that the side arguing “no” always wins. Items 9–12 (editing, rubric, and harder evaluation items) can be assigned for homework.

Checks for understanding

  1. “Is the Extended Response asking which side you agree with?” Expected: No; which side is better supported by its evidence.
  2. “Name the three rubric traits.” Expected: Arguments and evidence; development and organization; clarity and command of standard English.
  3. “Why is Bell’s 1,200-jobs number weak even though it is specific?” Expected: The team paid for the study and gains from the result; Osei shows the jobs are mostly part-time and seasonal.
  4. “What three things does a strong thesis do?” Expected: Names the better-supported side, gives reasons, refers to both authors.
  5. “What does each body paragraph need after a quotation?” Expected: An explanation of why the evidence is strong or weak.

Common mistakes and how to correct them

Arguing a personal opinion. (“Ballparks are fun, so we should build one.”) Correct by asking, “Which author proved it better?” Ban “I believe the city should…” and replace it with “Osei’s argument is better supported because…”

Summarizing instead of evaluating. Essays that retell each article earn little on Trait 1. Require a judgment word in every body paragraph: strong, weak, reliable, biased, specific, vague, unsupported.

Using only one passage. The prompt requires evidence from both. The organizer has two columns for a reason; neither may be empty.

“Both sides have good points.” Fairness is good in the counterargument paragraph, but the thesis must choose.

Dropping quotations without explanation. Teach the P-E-E-L pattern and require at least one “This shows…” sentence after each quotation.

Judging by length, tone, or title. A longer, more emotional, or more confident passage is not automatically better supported. Count and test the evidence.

Informal language. (“Bell’s argument is kinda weak.”) Trait 2 includes formal style. Offer replacements: “less convincing,” “poorly supported,” “relies on.”

Differentiation

Support: Give sentence frames: “___’s argument is better supported because ___, while ___ relies on ___.” “In paragraph __, ___ states that ‘___.’ This evidence is strong/weak because ___.” Let learners work only on body paragraph 1 at first. Read passages aloud and stop after each paragraph to ask, “Evidence or opinion?”

Stretch: Have learners write the counterargument paragraph for the turf passages, find one weakness in the stronger passage (for example, Osei does not name the studies), or plan a response arguing for Bell and discover how much harder it is to support.

Teacher note: The ballpark passages are used for teaching and the model response. The turf passages are reserved for the practice items so learners meet a pair they have not already discussed. In Week 10, learners will write a full timed response.

How this shows up on the GED

The Extended Response appears in the RLA test as a separate 45-minute section. Learners see two passages (often an article and a response, or two opinion pieces) and the standard prompt asking which position is best supported. They type in a plain text box with basic editing tools (cut, copy, paste, undo, redo); there is no spell-check. The essay is a significant part of the RLA score, so a blank or off-topic response is very costly.

The same skills appear in multiple-choice reading items with paired passages. Expect wording such as:

  • “Which evidence from the passage best supports the author’s claim that …?”
  • “Which statement from Passage B is not supported by evidence?”
  • “How does the author of Passage A respond to the concern that …?”
  • “Which two statements identify faulty reasoning in the letter?” (multiple select)
  • Hot spot items: “Click the sentence that provides the strongest evidence for …”
  • Drag-and-drop items sorting statements into evidence vs. opinion, or Passage A vs. Passage B.
student:
What the Extended Response asks you to do

On the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts test, you will have 45 minutes to read two passages that take opposite sides on an issue and type an essay about them. The prompt will look like this:

In your response, analyze both positions presented in the articles to determine which one is best supported. Use relevant and specific evidence from both articles to support your response.

Notice what the prompt does not ask. It does not ask what you think about the issue. It asks which author did a better job of proving their point. You might personally disagree with the better-supported side, and that is fine. Your job is to be the judge, not a player.

How your essay is scored

TraitWhat scorers look forPoints
1. Creation of arguments and use of evidenceA clear position on which argument is better supported; specific, relevant evidence from both passages; explanation of why the evidence is strong or weak0–2
2. Development of ideas and organizational structureAn introduction, body paragraphs, and conclusion; ideas that build logically; transitions; a formal, serious tone0–2
3. Clarity and command of standard EnglishClear, varied sentences; mostly correct grammar, spelling, capitalization, and punctuation. A few small errors are expected in a timed draft.0–2

An essay that only shares your opinion, or does not use the passages, will score low on Trait 1 even if it is beautifully written.

How to decide which side is better supported

Test each piece of evidence with five questions:

  1. Source: Who says so? Are they an expert? Are they named? Do they gain something from the outcome?
  2. Specific: Are there numbers, dates, or measurements, or just words like “many” and “everyone”?
  3. Relevant: Does it prove this claim, or something else?
  4. Sufficient: Is there enough? One story is not a pattern.
  5. Fair: Does the author deal honestly with the other side?

Also watch for faulty reasoning: hasty generalization (one example becomes a rule), bandwagon (“everyone agrees”), slippery slope (one step will lead to disaster), and emotional appeals used in place of evidence.

Do not judge a passage by how long, confident, or emotional it is. Count and test the evidence.

Practice pair: the Port Delaney ballpark

Read both passages. Highlight strong evidence in one color and weak evidence or appeals in another.

Passage A: Build the Ballpark and Bring Downtown Back

By Marcus Bell, President, Port Delaney Downtown Business Association

[1] For twenty years, the old rail yard on Front Street has been an empty lot surrounded by a chain-link fence. Now we have a chance to turn it into the best thing to happen to Port Delaney in a generation. The Port Delaney Pelicans, our minor league baseball team, have offered to move into a new downtown ballpark if the city provides $48 million to build it. The city council should say yes.

[2] A ballpark would create jobs and spending. A study commissioned by the Pelicans found that the new ballpark would create 1,200 jobs and bring $30 million a year into the local economy. Restaurants, bars, and shops near the park would be full every game night.

[3] We have all seen what a ballpark can do. My brother-in-law lives in Harlan City, which opened a new stadium in 2015. He says downtown Harlan City is now packed with new restaurants and apartments. If it worked for Harlan City, it will work for us.

[4] The team’s current lease ends in two years. The Pelicans’ owners have said publicly that they will consider offers from other cities if Port Delaney does not build a new park. Losing our team would be a blow to the city’s pride and to the hundreds of families who attend games each summer.

[5] Some critics complain about the cost. But the ballpark will pay for itself many times over. Everyone I talk to downtown is excited about this project, and the people of Port Delaney deserve a city they can be proud of. Let’s play ball.

Passage B: A Ballpark Is a Bad Bet for Taxpayers

By Dr. Elaine Osei, Professor of Economics, Port Delaney Community College

[1] A downtown ballpark sounds exciting, and I understand why many residents want one. But before the city council commits $48 million in public money, residents should look at what the evidence says about stadium deals.

[2] Economists have studied publicly funded stadiums in dozens of cities over more than thirty years. These independent studies have reached a consistent conclusion: new stadiums rarely produce meaningful growth in local jobs or income. One main reason is that most fans are local residents. A family that spends $120 at a ballgame usually spends that money instead of going to a movie, a restaurant, or a bowling alley elsewhere in town. The spending moves around; it does not grow.

[3] The study the Pelicans paid for claims the ballpark will create 1,200 jobs. Yet the team plays about 70 home games a year. Most ballpark jobs, such as ushers, ticket takers, and food workers, are part-time and seasonal. The study does not say how many of the 1,200 jobs would be full-time or year-round, and because it was paid for by the team, it should be read with caution.

[4] The cost to residents is clear. To raise the $48 million, the city would sell bonds and repay about $3.1 million a year for 25 years, a total of about $77.5 million. The ballpark’s lease, as proposed, would return only about $400,000 a year to the city in rent. That $3.1 million a year is more than the city’s entire yearly budget for road repair.

[5] Losing the Pelicans would disappoint many fans, me included. But if the team truly benefits from a new park, the owners should pay most of the cost. The city could offer the Front Street land and help with roads and parking. Taxpayers should not carry the risk for a private business.

Worked example 1: Test one piece of evidence

Bell, paragraph 2: “A study commissioned by the Pelicans found that the new ballpark would create 1,200 jobs and bring $30 million a year into the local economy.”

  • Source: The team paid for the study, and the team gets the ballpark. The source may be biased.
  • Specific: Yes, it has numbers. But specific is not the same as reliable.
  • Check the other passage: Osei says the team plays about 70 home games, most ballpark jobs are part-time and seasonal, and the study never says how many jobs are full-time.

Verdict: Weak evidence.

Worked example 2: Write a thesis

A strong thesis (1) names the better-supported side, (2) gives the reasons, and (3) mentions both authors.

  • “I think the ballpark is a waste of money.” Weak: personal opinion.
  • “Both authors make good points.” Weak: no position.
  • “Osei’s argument is better supported because she relies on independent research and specific cost figures, while Bell relies on a team-funded study, one personal story, and appeals to pride.” Strong.

The strong thesis is also your plan: one body paragraph on Bell’s weak evidence, one on Osei’s strong evidence.

Worked example 3: Build a body paragraph with P-E-E-L

Point: Osei supports her cost claim with clear numbers.
Evidence: She explains that the city would repay about $3.1 million a year for 25 years, about $77.5 million in all, while collecting only about $400,000 a year in rent.
Explain: These figures are specific and can be checked, and they show the city would pay far more than it gets back.
Link: In contrast, Bell says the ballpark will “pay for itself many times over” but never shows how.

Plan before you write: a sample organizer

Spend about 10 minutes planning. It saves time when you write.

Passage A (Bell)Passage B (Osei)
ClaimThe city should pay $48 million for a downtown ballpark.The city should not pay for the ballpark; the team should pay most of the cost.
Key evidenceTeam-paid study: 1,200 jobs, $30 million a year (para. 2); brother-in-law in Harlan City (para. 3); lease ends in two years (para. 4)30+ years of independent studies (para. 2); $120 family example (para. 2); 70 home games, part-time jobs (para. 3); $3.1 million a year for 25 years = $77.5 million vs. $400,000 rent (para. 4)
QualityWeak. Study paid for by the team; one secondhand story; “pay for itself” has no numbers.Strong. Independent research; specific, checkable numbers; directly answers Bell’s job claim.
Flaws or appealsHasty generalization (Harlan City); bandwagon (“Everyone I talk to”); appeal to prideFew. Does not give the names of the studies, but describes them clearly.
Counterargument?Waves off cost critics without numbers.Admits fans would be disappointed; offers a middle path (land, roads, parking).

Thesis: Osei’s argument is better supported because she relies on independent research and specific cost figures, while Bell relies on a team-funded study, one personal story, and appeals to pride.

Body 1 (A’s weaknesses): team-paid study; Harlan City story; “everyone I talk to.”
Body 2 (B’s strengths): independent studies; spending moves around; $77.5 million vs. $400,000 rent; answers the 1,200-jobs claim.
Body 3 (fairness): Bell’s best point (team could leave) and how Osei answers it.
Conclusion: restate thesis in new words.

A model response

Here is what a high-scoring response to the ballpark passages could look like. Notice the thesis at the end of the first paragraph, one paragraph per job, quotations followed by explanations, and a fair look at the other side.

Model response (would earn 2 points on each trait)

Port Delaney must decide whether to spend $48 million in public money on a new downtown ballpark for its minor league team, the Pelicans. Marcus Bell, president of the Downtown Business Association, argues that the ballpark would bring jobs and life back to downtown. Dr. Elaine Osei, an economics professor, argues that the deal is a bad bet for taxpayers. After analyzing both articles, I find that Osei’s position is better supported, because she uses independent research and specific cost figures, while Bell depends on a study paid for by the team, one secondhand story, and appeals to pride.

Bell’s strongest-sounding evidence is weaker than it first appears. He states that the ballpark would create 1,200 jobs and bring in $30 million a year, but this number comes from “a study commissioned by the Pelicans,” the same team that would receive the new park. A source that profits from the result has a reason to make the numbers look good. Bell also points to his brother-in-law, who says downtown Harlan City is “packed” since its stadium opened. One relative’s impression of one city is not enough to prove what will happen in Port Delaney. Finally, Bell claims the park “will pay for itself many times over” and that “everyone I talk to downtown is excited,” but he gives no figures to back up the first claim, and the second is a popularity appeal, not evidence.

Osei, on the other hand, supports each of her claims with specific evidence. She explains that economists have studied publicly funded stadiums “in dozens of cities over more than thirty years” and found that they “rarely produce meaningful growth in local jobs or income.” She also explains why: a family that spends $120 at a game usually spends it instead of going somewhere else in town, so “the spending moves around; it does not grow.” She directly answers Bell’s job claim by noting that the team plays only about 70 home games a year, so most ballpark jobs are part-time and seasonal. Her cost figures are clear and can be checked: the city would repay about $3.1 million a year for 25 years, about $77.5 million in all, while collecting only about $400,000 a year in rent.

To be fair, Bell raises one real concern. The team’s lease ends in two years, and the owners have said they may consider other cities. However, Osei does not ignore this risk. She admits that losing the team “would disappoint many fans, me included,” and she offers a middle path in which the city provides land, roads, and parking while the owners pay most of the cost. Because she responds to the other side instead of brushing it off, her argument is more credible.

In the end, Osei builds her case on independent research, clear numbers, and a fair response to the opposing view. Bell builds his on a team-funded study, a family member’s opinion, and civic pride. For these reasons, Osei’s argument is the better supported of the two.

Your 45 minutes

MinutesStep
About 10Read both passages, highlight, fill in the organizer, write your thesis
About 28Type the introduction, 2–3 body paragraphs, and a conclusion
About 7Reread, fix errors, make sure you used both passages

Try it

1. Bell writes, “Everyone I talk to downtown is excited about this project.” What type of faulty reasoning is this, and why is it weak?

Show answer

It is a bandwagon appeal. How many people are excited does not prove the ballpark will create jobs or pay for itself, and “everyone I talk to” is a small, unnamed group.

2. Which evidence in Osei’s passage directly answers Bell’s claim of 1,200 jobs?

Show answer

Paragraph 3: the team plays only about 70 home games a year, most ballpark jobs are part-time and seasonal, and the team-paid study does not say how many jobs are full-time or year-round.

3. Rewrite this weak thesis so it would score well: “Both articles make good points about the ballpark.”

Show answer

Sample: “Although both authors care about Port Delaney, Osei’s argument is better supported because her claims rest on independent research and clear cost figures, while Bell’s rest on a study paid for by the team and a relative’s opinion.” Any thesis that picks a side, gives reasons, and mentions both authors is correct.

4. A learner writes, “Bell’s evidence is kinda weak cuz his brother in law aint an expert.” Which trait does this sentence hurt most, and how would you fix it?

Show answer

Trait 3 (and the formal style part of Trait 2). The idea is good, but the language is informal and incorrect. Fix: “Bell’s evidence is weak because his brother-in-law is not an expert, and one person’s impression of one city does not prove a pattern.”

5. What is Bell’s strongest point, and how does Osei respond to it?

Show answer

His strongest point is that the lease ends in two years and the owners have said publicly they may consider other cities (paragraph 4). Osei admits losing the team “would disappoint many fans, me included,” and proposes that the city offer land, roads, and parking while the owners pay most of the cost.
post:
Summary of key points

  • The Extended Response asks which of two arguments is better supported, not which side you agree with.
  • Each of the three traits is scored 0–2: (1) arguments and use of evidence, (2) development and organization, (3) clarity and command of standard English.
  • Test evidence with five questions: source, specific, relevant, sufficient, fair. Specific is not the same as reliable; check who paid for or benefits from the evidence.
  • Watch for faulty reasoning: hasty generalization, bandwagon, slippery slope, emotional appeals in place of proof, unsupported claims.
  • A strong thesis names the better-supported side, gives reasons, and mentions both authors.
  • Plan for about 10 minutes with a two-column organizer, and use evidence from both passages.
  • Build body paragraphs with P-E-E-L: Point, Evidence, Explain, Link.

Exit ticket

1. True or false: You should choose the side you personally agree with.

Show answer

False. Choose the side whose evidence is stronger.

2. A passage quotes “a survey by the company selling the product.” Which of the five questions raises a concern?

Show answer

Source. The company benefits from good results, so the survey may be biased.

3. What is wrong with this thesis: “Passage B is better.”

Show answer

It gives no reasons and does not name the authors or what makes Passage B stronger.

4. What comes after the Evidence step in a P-E-E-L paragraph, and why does it matter?

Show answer

Explain. Saying why the evidence is strong or weak is how you earn Trait 1 points.

5. “If we allow one food truck downtown, soon the streets will be full of them.” Name the flaw.

Show answer

Slippery slope.

Reflection

  1. Think about a time someone tried to convince you of something. What kind of evidence actually changed your mind?
  2. Which of the five evidence questions is hardest for you to remember to ask? How will you remind yourself on test day?
  3. Which part of the 45 minutes worries you most: reading, planning, writing, or checking? What will you practice this week to get more comfortable?

Day 2Complete practice items 1–6. Read every explanation.30 min
Day 3Complete practice items 7–12. Then fill in a full planning organizer for the turf passages and write a thesis.35 min
Day 4Using your turf organizer, type one body paragraph (P-E-E-L) in 12 minutes without spell-check. Check it against the rubric.30 min
Day 5Take this week’s Practice GED for Reasoning Through Language Arts under timed conditions, including the Extended Response.40 min, continue on Day 6
Day 6Finish the Practice GED. Score your essay with the three traits and list one goal for each trait.40 min

Test-taking strategy: Write the thesis before the essay

Do not start typing your introduction until your thesis is written down in your organizer. If you can finish the sentence “___’s argument is better supported because ___, while ___ relies on ___,” you already have your introduction’s last line and your body paragraph topics. If you cannot finish it, go back to the passages for two more minutes; that is much faster than rewriting an essay that wanders.

vocab.def: The 45-minute typed essay on the GED RLA test in which you analyze two opposing arguments and explain which one is better supported.
vocab.example: For the Extended Response, I read two articles about a ballpark and wrote about which was better supported.

vocab.def: A piece of writing that tries to convince readers to accept a position by giving reasons and evidence.
vocab.example: Osei's argument is that taxpayers should not pay for the ballpark.

vocab.def: The main position an author wants readers to accept.
vocab.example: Bell's claim: the city should pay $48 million for a ballpark.

vocab.def: Facts, numbers, research, examples, or expert statements that an author uses to prove a claim.
vocab.example: Repaying $3.1 million a year for 25 years is evidence about cost.

vocab.def: The explanation that connects evidence to a claim and shows why the evidence proves it.
vocab.example: Fans mostly live in town, so their spending moves around instead of growing.

vocab.def: Backed by evidence that is more reliable, specific, relevant, and sufficient than the other side's evidence.
vocab.example: Osei's position is better supported because her evidence is independent and specific.

vocab.def: How believable and trustworthy a source or author is.
vocab.example: An independent economist has more credibility on stadium costs than a study paid for by the team.

vocab.def: A slant toward one side, often because the source gains something from a particular result.
vocab.example: A study paid for by the team that wants the ballpark may be biased.

vocab.def: A short personal story used as evidence; it can make a point vivid but cannot prove a pattern by itself.
vocab.example: Bell's story about his brother-in-law in Harlan City is an anecdote.

vocab.def: Faulty reasoning that draws a broad conclusion from too few examples.
vocab.example: "It worked in one city, so it will work everywhere."

vocab.def: Faulty reasoning that says something must be right because many people support it.
vocab.example: "Everyone I talk to downtown is excited."

vocab.def: A point that goes against an author's position; strong writers acknowledge it and respond to it.
vocab.example: Osei admits losing the team would disappoint fans, then offers another plan.

vocab.def: One sentence, usually at the end of the introduction, that states which argument is better supported and why.
vocab.example: Osei's argument is better supported because she relies on independent research and specific cost figures.

vocab.def: One of the three qualities the GED essay rubric scores, each from 0 to 2 points.
vocab.example: Trait 1 is creation of arguments and use of evidence.

notes:
Week 9 RLA Study Sheet: The Extended Response I

The task

  • 45 minutes, typed, two opposing passages
  • Decide which position is better supported (not which you agree with)
  • Use specific evidence from both passages

The rubric (each trait 0–2)

  1. Arguments and evidence: clear position; specific, relevant evidence from both texts; explain why it is strong or weak
  2. Development and organization: intro, body, conclusion; logical order; transitions; formal tone
  3. Clarity and standard English: clear, varied sentences; correct grammar and punctuation

Five evidence questions

  1. Source: who, expert, independent?
  2. Specific: numbers, dates, named studies?
  3. Relevant: proves this claim?
  4. Sufficient: enough, or one story?
  5. Fair: deals with the other side?

Red flags

  • Hasty generalization: one case → rule
  • Bandwagon: “everyone agrees”
  • Slippery slope: one step → disaster
  • Emotional appeal in place of proof
  • Unnamed source: “I read online”
  • Source that profits from the result

Thesis frame

___’s argument is better supported because ___, while ___ relies on ___.

P-E-E-L body paragraph

Point → Evidence (quote or paraphrase) → Explain (why strong or weak) → Link (back to thesis or other passage)

Essay plan and timing

StepJob
Plan (~10 min)Read, highlight, organizer, thesis
IntroductionIssue, both authors’ positions, thesis
Body 1Weaknesses of the weaker passage
Body 2Strengths of the stronger passage
Body 3 (optional)Best point of the weaker side and how the stronger side answers it
ConclusionRestate thesis in new words (writing total ~28 min)
Check (~7 min)Both passages used? Errors fixed?

Judgment words to use: strong, weak, reliable, biased, specific, vague, unsupported, credible, relies on, fails to.

stimuli.title: Passage A: More Playing Time for Millbrook: Why Corbin Park Needs Turf Fields
stimuli.html:
By Dana Whitfield, Director, Millbrook Parks and Recreation Department

[1] Every spring, the same scene plays out at Corbin Park. Parents pull into the parking lot, children pile out with their cleats on, and they find a sign taped to the gate: FIELDS CLOSED, TOO WET. The city council will soon vote on a plan to convert the park’s two main grass fields to artificial turf. I urge the council to approve it. Turf would give our young people far more time to play, and it would save water and money.

[2] Grass fields have served Millbrook well for decades, but they have a serious limit. When grass is wet, cleats tear up the roots, so the fields must close after heavy rain. Last year, the two main fields at Corbin Park were closed on 46 days, mostly during the spring and fall league seasons. Every closure means canceled practices, rescheduled games, and frustrated families. An artificial turf field drains quickly and can be used again within an hour of a storm.

[3] Because grass needs time to recover, we also limit how many hours each field can be used. Our department’s scheduling records show that the two fields were available for about 1,100 hours of play last year. With turf, we could schedule them for more than 3,000 hours. That extra time matters. This fall, our youth soccer and football leagues turned away 210 children because there was no field space for more teams.

[4] Turf would also save resources. Last summer, the two fields used 1.3 million gallons of water, during a season when residents were asked to limit lawn watering. Mowing, fertilizing, lining, and reseeding the two fields cost the city $58,000. Turf fields need brushing and cleaning, which we estimate at about $12,000 a year, for savings of roughly $46,000 a year.

[5] I want to be honest about the drawbacks. Turf is not cheap. The conversion will cost $2.2 million, and a regional recreation grant will cover half. A turf surface also wears out and must be replaced after about ten years, at a cost of about $450,000 per field. Our yearly savings would cover about half of that future cost, not all of it.

[6] Turf also gets hotter than grass in direct summer sun. We plan to address this in three ways: using a light-colored infill that stays cooler than black rubber, adding shade structures beside both fields, and having staff check the surface temperature with a handheld thermometer on summer afternoons. If the surface reaches 120 degrees, play will pause until it cools.

[7] No playing surface is perfect. But turf would let hundreds more children play, conserve water, and lower yearly costs. The council should vote yes.

stimuli.title: Passage B: Keep Corbin Park Green
stimuli.html:
Letter to the Editor, by Gary Pruitt, Millbrook resident and volunteer youth soccer coach

[1] I have coached youth soccer at Corbin Park for six years, and I am asking the city council to vote no on the plan to rip out our grass fields and replace them with plastic.

[2] Last spring, my son played an away game on a turf field in another town. He slid for a ball and came home with a burn on his leg the size of my hand. If turf could do that to my son in one game, imagine what it will do to hundreds of kids every week. A coach I know from a neighboring league told me that injuries on his team doubled after his town switched to turf.

[3] Turf also gets dangerously hot. Last July, a local news crew measured the surface of a turf field at Lakeview High School at 152 degrees on a 90-degree afternoon. Grass a few yards away measured 95 degrees. Our kids should not have to play on a surface that hot.

[4] Then there are the health risks. I have read online that turf is full of toxic chemicals, and I would not want my children breathing them in. Why take the chance?

[5] Supporters say turf will save money, but they leave out the replacement costs. Turf wears out, and the city will have to pay millions every few years to replace it. That money could go to our schools instead.

[6] Yes, the grass fields close sometimes after a big rain. But kids have been playing on grass at Corbin Park for seventy years. My grandfather played on this grass, and so should my grandchildren. And make no mistake: once the city puts down plastic fields, the next step will be paving the rest of the park for parking lots.

[7] Corbin Park is the heart of Millbrook. Keep it green.

stimuli.title: A Student's Draft Body Paragraph (contains errors)
stimuli.html: (1) Whitfield’s argument is better supported because she uses city records and addresses the concerns about turf. (2) Whitfield supports her claim with official records. (A), she reports that the two main fields were closed on 46 days last year and that the leagues turned away 210 children. (3) Her figures on water use and maintenance costs (B) also specific and could be checked. (4) Pruitt, on the other hand, relies mostly on stories and fears. (5) His claim about toxic chemicals (C) because he never names a source. (6) Overall, Pruitt’s evidence is weaker (D) Whitfield’s.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses Whitfield’s main claim in Passage A?
options: Millbrook should convert the two main Corbin Park fields to artificial turf because turf would allow much more playing time and would save water and money.
Artificial turf is safer than grass in every way, so all parks in Millbrook should replace their grass.
Millbrook should build new fields in another park so that Corbin Park can rest after heavy rain.
The city should water the Corbin Park fields less often to save money during dry summers.
items.hint: Look at the end of paragraph 1 and at paragraph 7, where Whitfield states what she wants the council to do and why.
items.explain:
Step 1: Find where the author states her position. In paragraph 1 she writes, “I urge the council to approve it. Turf would give our young people far more time to play, and it would save water and money.” Paragraph 7 repeats this: “The council should vote yes.”

Step 2: The correct choice includes both the position (convert two fields) and her reasons (more playing time, water and money savings).

The “safer than grass in every way” choice is a distortion: Whitfield admits turf gets hotter (paragraph 6) and never says it is safer or that every park should change. Building new fields elsewhere and watering less are never proposed.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses Pruitt’s position in Passage B?
options: The city council should reject the turf plan and keep natural grass at Corbin Park.
The city should delay the turf plan until scientists finish more studies.
The city should install turf on one field and keep grass on the other.
The city should spend the turf money on shade structures for the grass fields.
items.hint: What does Pruitt ask the council to do in paragraph 1, and what does he say in his last sentence?
items.explain:
Step 1: In paragraph 1 Pruitt says he is “asking the city council to vote no on the plan.” Step 2: In paragraph 7 he ends, “Keep it green.” So his position is to reject the plan and keep grass.

He never asks for more studies, a compromise with one turf field, or shade structures. (Shade structures come from Whitfield’s passage, paragraph 6.) He suggests the money could go to schools, not to shade.

items.prompt: Whitfield claims that grass fields limit how often children can play. Click the sentence from paragraph 2 that provides the most specific evidence for this claim.
spans: Grass fields have served Millbrook well for decades, but they have a serious limit.
When grass is wet, cleats tear up the roots, so the fields must close after heavy rain.
Last year, the two main fields at Corbin Park were closed on 46 days, mostly during the spring and fall league seasons.
Every closure means canceled practices, rescheduled games, and frustrated families.
An artificial turf field drains quickly and can be used again within an hour of a storm.
items.hint: Specific evidence usually includes a number, a date, or a measurement that could be checked.
items.explain:
Step 1: Look for a sentence with a fact that could be checked. Step 2: Only the third sentence gives a measured fact about the Corbin Park fields: they “were closed on 46 days” last year.

The first sentence is a general claim. The second explains why fields close (reasoning) but gives no measurement. The fourth describes effects in general words. The fifth is about turf, not about how grass limits play.

items.prompt: Why is the news crew’s measurement in paragraph 3 of Passage B stronger evidence than the coach’s statement in paragraph 2?
options: It comes from an identified source and reports specific measurements that readers could check.
It appeals more strongly to readers’ feelings about the safety of children.
It is about Corbin Park itself, while the coach’s statement is about a different town.
It is longer and includes more detail about the coach’s team.
items.hint: Ask two of the evidence questions: Who is the source? Is the evidence specific?
items.explain:
Step 1: The coach is unnamed (“A coach I know”), and his claim that injuries “doubled” is secondhand with no numbers or records. Step 2: The news crew is an identified source (a local news crew at Lakeview High School) and reports exact readings: 152 degrees on turf and 95 degrees on grass on a 90-degree afternoon. Step 3: Named, specific, checkable evidence is stronger.

The Corbin Park choice is wrong because the measurement was taken at Lakeview High School, not Corbin Park. Emotional appeal does not make evidence stronger, and length is not a measure of quality.

items.prompt: Which two statements identify faulty reasoning in Pruitt’s letter? Select two answers.
options: He predicts that installing turf will lead to paving the rest of the park for parking lots, without evidence that this is planned.
He uses one injury to his son in one game to predict what will happen to hundreds of children every week.
He cites a specific temperature measurement taken by a local news crew.
He admits that the grass fields sometimes close after a big rain.
He states that turf can be hotter than grass on summer afternoons.
items.hint: Look for a prediction that jumps from one step to a disaster, and a conclusion based on a single example.
items.explain:
Correct: The parking-lot prediction (paragraph 6) is a slippery slope: Pruitt claims one step will lead to a much worse result but gives no evidence. Using his son’s single burn to predict harm to “hundreds of kids every week” (paragraph 2) is a hasty generalization.

Not faulty: The news crew measurement is specific evidence. Admitting the fields close after rain is a concession, which is fair reasoning. The claim that turf can be hotter is supported by the measurement, and Whitfield agrees with it in paragraph 6.

items.prompt: How does Whitfield respond to the concern that turf gets hot in summer?
options: She admits that turf gets hotter than grass and describes specific steps the city will take to reduce the risk.
She argues that the heat is not a real problem because children are used to playing in summer weather.
She claims that studies showing turf is hotter than grass were paid for by grass companies.
She says the fields will be closed for the entire summer so that heat will not matter.
items.hint: Reread paragraph 6. Does she deny the problem or accept it?
items.explain:
Step 1: In paragraph 6, Whitfield writes, “Turf also gets hotter than grass in direct summer sun.” She accepts the concern. Step 2: She lists three steps: light-colored infill, shade structures, and temperature checks, with play pausing at 120 degrees.

She never dismisses the heat, never attacks studies, and never says the fields will close all summer. Acknowledging a problem and offering a solution makes an argument more credible.

items.prompt: The statements below come from Passage A and Passage B. Drag each statement into the correct category.
choices: Last year, the two main fields at Corbin Park were closed on 46 days. (Passage A)
Mowing, fertilizing, lining, and reseeding the two fields cost the city $58,000. (Passage A)
A local news crew measured a turf field at 152 degrees while nearby grass measured 95 degrees. (Passage B)
I have read online that turf is full of toxic chemicals. (Passage B)
My grandfather played on this grass, and so should my grandchildren. (Passage B)
Once the city puts down plastic fields, the next step will be paving the rest of the park. (Passage B)
items.hint: Ask of each statement: Is there a named source or a number someone could check? Or is it a feeling, a rumor, or a prediction with no proof?
items.explain:
Specific, checkable evidence: The 46 closure days and the $58,000 cost come from the parks department’s own records and include exact figures. The 152-degree and 95-degree readings come from an identified news crew at a named school. Notice that strong evidence can appear in either passage.

Unsupported claim or emotional appeal: “I have read online” names no source and gives no facts. The grandfather sentence appeals to tradition and feelings, not evidence. The paving prediction is a slippery slope with no proof that such a plan exists.

items.prompt: A student is planning an Extended Response about Passage A and Passage B. Which thesis statement would best begin a high-scoring response?
options: Whitfield’s argument is better supported because she backs her claims with city records on closures, costs, and water use and directly addresses the heat concern, while Pruitt relies mostly on one story, secondhand claims, and fears.
I think artificial turf is better than grass because I have played on it and it never gets muddy.
Both Whitfield and Pruitt make good points about Corbin Park, and the city council will have a hard decision.
Pruitt’s argument is better supported because he is a coach and cares more about children than Whitfield does.
items.hint: A strong thesis names the better-supported side, gives reasons based on the evidence, and mentions both authors.
items.explain:
Step 1: The thesis must answer the prompt: which position is better supported. Step 2: It should give reasons drawn from the evidence. Step 3: It should refer to both passages.

The correct choice does all three. The “I have played on it” choice is personal opinion and uses no evidence from the passages. The “both make good points” choice takes no position. The last choice picks a side but supports it with an assumption about who “cares more,” which is not evidence and is not stated in either passage.

items.prompt:
Read the student’s draft paragraph. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank in these sentences.

Sentence 2: Whitfield supports her claim with official records. {{0}}, she reports that the two main fields were closed on 46 days last year and that the leagues turned away 210 children.

Sentence 3: Her figures on water use and maintenance costs {{1}} also specific and could be checked.

Sentence 5: His claim about toxic chemicals {{2}} because he never names a source.

Sentence 6: Overall, Pruitt’s evidence is weaker {{3}} Whitfield’s.

options: For example
However
In contrast
Otherwise
is
are
was
has been
is kinda sketchy
is less convincing
totally fails
is no good at all
then
than
that
as

items.hint: (A) Does the sentence give an example or a contrast? (B) Find the subject: is it singular or plural? (C) Which choice sounds formal? (D) Which word is used for comparisons?
items.explain:
Blank (A): Sentence 2 states that Whitfield uses official records; the next part gives instances of those records. A transition that introduces an example is needed: For example. “However” and “In contrast” signal an opposite idea, and “Otherwise” signals an alternative, so they do not fit.

Blank (B): The subject is “figures” (not “costs,” which is part of the phrase “on water use and maintenance costs”). “Figures” is plural, and the paragraph is in present tense, so the verb is are. “Is,” “was,” and “has been” are singular.

Blank (C): An essay needs a formal, precise tone (part of Trait 2). is less convincing is formal. “Kinda sketchy” and “no good at all” are informal, and “totally fails” is an exaggeration in casual language.

Blank (D): Use than to compare (“weaker than”). “Then” refers to time. “That” and “as” do not complete a comparison with “weaker.”

items.prompt: A student argues that Whitfield’s position is better supported. Which detail from Pruitt’s letter could the student most effectively show to be inaccurate by using information from Whitfield’s passage?
options: Pruitt’s claim that supporters “leave out the replacement costs” and that the city will pay “millions every few years,” since Whitfield states the replacement cost and says the surface lasts about ten years
Pruitt’s report that a news crew measured a turf field at 152 degrees, since Whitfield says turf never gets hotter than 120 degrees
Pruitt’s statement that he has coached youth soccer at Corbin Park for six years, since Whitfield says the leagues turned away 210 children
Pruitt’s description of Corbin Park as “the heart of Millbrook,” since Whitfield says the park’s fields are closed often
items.hint: Find a statement by Pruitt about something Whitfield discusses directly with specific facts. Then check whether her facts contradict him.
items.explain:
Step 1: In paragraph 5, Pruitt says supporters “leave out the replacement costs” and that the city will pay “millions every few years.” Step 2: In her paragraph 5, Whitfield does discuss replacement: the surface lasts “about ten years” and costs “about $450,000 per field.” For two fields, that is 2 × $450,000 = $900,000 about every ten years, not millions every few years. Step 3: So Whitfield’s facts directly contradict both parts of Pruitt’s claim.

The 152-degree choice misreads Whitfield: 120 degrees is the temperature at which play will pause, not a limit on how hot turf can get. She agrees turf gets hot. Pruitt’s coaching experience and his description of the park are not contradicted by anything in Passage A.

items.prompt:
Read this paragraph from a student’s Extended Response about the turf passages.

Artificial turf is the right choice for Millbrook. When I was in high school, our team played on turf, and we never had to cancel a game because of mud. Furthermore, turf looks bright and clean all year, while grass turns brown in August. In addition, young people today need more places to exercise, and turf fields can be used in almost any weather. For these reasons, the city should install turf as soon as possible.

Which rubric trait does this paragraph most need to improve, and why?
options: Trait 1, because it argues the writer’s own opinion with personal experience instead of evaluating the evidence in the two passages
Trait 3, because it contains many errors in grammar, spelling, and punctuation
Trait 2, because it has no transitions connecting its ideas
None, because it states a clear position and gives three reasons
items.hint: Check what the paragraph uses as evidence. Does it mention Whitfield, Pruitt, or anything from their passages?
items.explain:
Step 1: Check Trait 3. The sentences are clear and correctly written, so Trait 3 is not the main problem. Step 2: Check Trait 2. The paragraph uses transitions (“Furthermore,” “In addition,” “For these reasons”) and has a clear order. Step 3: Check Trait 1. The paragraph never mentions either author or any evidence from the passages. It argues what the writer thinks the city should do, supported by the writer’s own high school experience. The task is to decide which passage is better supported, using evidence from both.

So Trait 1 needs the most improvement. A clear position with reasons is not enough when the reasons do not come from the texts.

items.prompt: In paragraph 5, Whitfield admits that “Our yearly savings would cover about half of that future cost, not all of it.” How does this admission most likely affect her argument?
options: It strengthens her credibility, because she honestly states a limitation and supports it with numbers, which makes her other figures more believable.
It destroys her argument, because she admits that turf will not completely pay for itself.
It shows that she agrees with Pruitt that the city cannot afford turf.
It has no effect on her argument, because cost is not related to her claim.
items.hint: Think about how readers react when an author admits a drawback openly instead of hiding it. Is cost part of her claim?
items.explain:
Step 1: Check the math she is describing. Savings: about $46,000 a year × 10 years = about $460,000. Replacement: 2 fields × $450,000 = $900,000. $460,000 is about half of $900,000, so her statement is accurate.

Step 2: Consider the effect. By stating a drawback openly with figures, Whitfield shows she is not hiding information, which makes her other numbers more trustworthy. Her main reasons (more playing time and lower yearly costs) still stand.

The “destroys her argument” choice overstates the effect: she never claimed turf would fully pay for itself. She does not agree the city cannot afford turf; she still urges a yes vote. Cost is related to her claim, because saving money is one of her main reasons.
